title: A medicine that holds its own therapeutic window without an external controller

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a medicine that senses a physiological signal and adjusts its own activity to keep a specified therapeutic effect within a specified safe and effective range. The sensing and response would be built into the drug or its formulation through chemical or physical mechanisms, without an external algorithm deciding when to increase or decrease treatment. Glucose-responsive insulin provides the clearest documented starting point: glucose supplies the signal, and insulin activity or availability responds to it.

For this record, the proposed scope includes individual responsive molecules, drug complexes and responsive delivery formulations such as depots. These are distinct implementations: a molecule can change its activity, whereas a formulation can change how much drug becomes available. Either could qualify if its internal response actually maintains the intended therapeutic effect. Merely releasing drug when a signal appears would not, by itself, demonstrate sustained control within a therapeutic window.

Scope synthesis: the defining capability is autonomous pharmacological feedback, rather than a particular insulin chemistry or delivery material. A medicine might respond to its own exposure or to the physiological variable it is intended to control, but exposure control and effect control are not interchangeable. The relevant endpoint must therefore be specified for each application. Demonstrating this capability for glucose would establish one application; extending it to coagulation, immunosuppression or chemotherapy would require additional advances.

significance.text: Successful human demonstration could establish internal feedback as a way to reduce dosing mismatch, potentially widening the useful therapeutic range of drugs for which too little treatment is ineffective and too much is dangerous. The direct benefit would be more appropriate activity as physiological demand changes within the system’s validated operating range. For insulin, the supplied commentary explicitly describes reducing excessive and insufficient dosing as a goal of glucose-responsive approaches.

External insulin-control systems already show that physiological feedback can guide treatment, and a self-adapting delivery algorithm has been reported feasible in adults with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Encoding the response in a medicine would move the control mechanism into the treatment itself. Conditional downstream synthesis: this could reduce dependence on external sensing and control hardware, including where such hardware is difficult to obtain or maintain, provided the medicine’s delivery, durability and safety are adequate.

Internal feedback would not automatically eliminate overdose or underdose. The commentary describes response delays, waning responsiveness and an initial hypoglycemic burst in experimental approaches. A sensor can detect the right signal while the resulting treatment still acts too late or too strongly. The revolutionary prospect is therefore reliable, bounded autonomous control, not immunity to dosing harm. Success with glucose would also not establish a universal solution for other drugs or physiological inputs.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is dependable coupling of physiological sensing to a sufficiently fast, durable and appropriately scaled therapeutic response in humans. Building a responsive component is only one part of that problem. The drug must retain useful potency and suitable pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics while its response remains effective across the intended treatment period. Brouillard’s 2025 commentary identifies relative-potency and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic limitations in the development history of MK-2640, alongside broader response and translation problems for glucose-responsive approaches.

Responsive formulations introduce material and delivery constraints as well as sensing constraints. Their components must be safe, their response must persist, and their release behavior must avoid harmful bursts or delays. Animal success must translate to human physiology and clinically usable delivery. Mechanistic synthesis: reducing further release may not promptly reverse the action of drug already released, so a convincing design must account for both the responsive mechanism and the subsequent duration of drug action.

Generality remains a separate research challenge. A glucose sensor does not automatically provide a suitable signal or control mechanism for anticoagulation, immune suppression or cancer treatment. Proposed engineering requirements for each extension include an informative input, a defined relationship between that input and the desired effect, and a response that can increase or decrease treatment on the necessary timescale. The supplied evidence does not establish these capabilities beyond glucose, nor does it establish the field-wide absence of internally responsive medicines as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: Wilkinson and colleagues reported a human feasibility study of automated insulin delivery using a self-adapting algorithm that required no meal announcement. The paper appeared online on July 3, 2025, and in the September 2026 issue of the Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology. The supplied review describes a single-arm, 12-week intervention with 42 enrolled adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Its abstract supports feasibility of external algorithm-based control; it does not establish definitive comparative efficacy or control encoded in a medicine.

Brouillard’s 2025 commentary describes glucose-responsive insulin approaches, including responsive analogs, complexes and delivery formulations. It reports that Merck’s investigational MK-2640 did not move forward because of limitations in relative potency and pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics. This is an attributed account of that product’s development history, rather than evidence that every route to internally controlled insulin has failed.

The commentary also summarizes animal results lasting about a week and experimental protection against intentional over-insulinization. These are meaningful precursors to the proposed capability, but they remain secondary reports in the supplied evidence: the underlying animal papers were not supplied for inspection. Their findings do not establish sustained human therapeutic-window control, and results from distinct formulations should not be combined into the performance profile of a single system.

The supplied review had a complete retained copy of the commentary, while the insulin-delivery study was available as an abstract record with figure captions rather than a full study report. The earlier account of a failed commentary reload therefore does not limit the review’s reading of that retained text. However, no bounded freshness search was supplied to establish approval status or field-wide availability as of November 1, 2026. The evidence supports the dated achievements above; it does not justify either declaring this innovation achieved or asserting that no qualifying medicine existed anywhere by that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed completion criterion: demonstrate in humans at least two drugs or drug formulations that sense different physiological inputs and each maintain a pre-specified therapeutic effect within a pre-specified window through internal control. The two-input requirement would test breadth beyond glucose; it is a proposed threshold for this innovation record, not an established scientific or regulatory standard. Neither an external sensor–algorithm–pump system nor an insulin demonstrated only in animals would satisfy it.
completion_criteria.label: Two drugs internally maintain prespecified therapeutic windows in humans using distinct inputs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration design: pre-specify the effect being controlled, target window, response time, treatment duration, allowable excursions and safety endpoints. Each demonstration should include an ethically controlled challenge that would be expected to cause excessive effect with a suitable nonresponsive comparator. The study should show that the internal response provides protection while preserving adequate treatment when demand rises. These tests should distinguish responsive control from simply using a weaker dose or releasing less drug overall.
completion_criteria.label: Internal responsiveness prevents excessive effects while preserving treatment under challenge

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the results independently and across relevant participants, manufacturing batches and physiological conditions. Characterize loss of responsiveness, delayed action, initial bursts and residual drug action after the signal changes. Report the delivery requirements, duration of useful control and conditions under which additional clinical intervention remains necessary. A finite test program would establish demonstrated breadth and operating limits, not literal universality across patients, drugs or disturbances.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes practical operating limits and delivery requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PHA-02, prospective prediction of human efficacy, dose and major toxicity, concerns anticipating treatment behavior before human exposure; PHA-13 concerns regulating treatment during use. PHA-03, prevention of idiosyncratic immune-mediated injury, addresses a different safety problem: keeping a conventional therapeutic effect within range would not by itself establish prevention of rare immune injury. PHA-10 seeks severe analgesia separated from respiratory depression and reinforcement. Responsive dosing could complement that goal, but would not establish the required separation of analgesic efficacy from those harms.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-05 seeks systemic access to brain parenchyma, and PHA-11 seeks reliable oral systemic exposure for folded peptides and proteins. Those entries address whether a drug reaches its destination or circulation; PHA-13 addresses how its activity adjusts after delivery. A responsive peptide formulation might need advances from both areas, but reliable access and autonomous control remain separate capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-01 concerns pharmacological control of proteins without usable binding pockets, while PHA-04 concerns antigen-chosen control of immune memory. Conditional activation could overlap technically with PHA-13, but selecting a target or activating treatment in a particular disease state does not by itself demonstrate feedback that maintains a therapeutic effect within a window.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-06, replacement of missing cell types; PHA-07, dismantling pathogenic protein conformations; PHA-08, eradication of dormant infectious persisters; PHA-09, changing aging rate across organs; and PHA-12, scarless regrowth of complex structures, define biological outcomes. Internal feedback could potentially help regulate treatments pursuing those outcomes, but achieving any one of them would not establish autonomous therapeutic-window control, and demonstrating PHA-13 would not establish those outcomes.

change_log.reason: The reviewed commentary covers several implementation types; restricting the concept to a single molecule would omit relevant approaches. Their mechanisms remain distinguished.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical elimination of dosing harms with conditional reduction within a validated operating range.
change_log.reason: Response delays, waning responsiveness and initial hypoglycemic bursts show that sensing alone does not guarantee safe control.

change_log.change: Removed the unsupported assertion that dosing across pharmacology is mostly open-loop and qualified claims of present-day absence or nonapproval.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence contains no field-wide survey or freshness search establishing those claims as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Added the insulin-device study’s online publication date, issue date, enrollment, duration and single-arm design.
change_log.reason: These details clarify chronology and distinguish a limited feasibility demonstration from comparative efficacy or medicine-encoded control.

change_log.change: Retained MK-2640’s reported development limitations and week-long animal results with their evidence boundaries.
change_log.reason: The commentary supports these attributed findings, but the underlying animal papers were not supplied and the product history does not establish failure of the entire concept.

change_log.change: Replaced the earlier browser-failure caveat with the access limitations documented by the validated review.
change_log.reason: The review had a complete retained commentary; the device study remained available only as an abstract record with figure captions.

change_log.change: Expanded the barriers to include response timing, durability, material safety, delivery behavior and animal-to-human translation.
change_log.reason: These useful review findings explain why a responsive component is insufficient for dependable therapeutic control.

change_log.reason: The two-drug threshold is not a consensus standard, and finite demonstrations establish bounded breadth rather than universality.

unresolved_issues: Approval status and field-wide availability as of November 1, 2026, remain unestablished by the supplied evidence.
The primary animal studies underlying the commentary’s week-long results and over-insulinization summaries were not supplied, leaving their detailed methods, reproducibility and limits unresolved.
The full insulin-delivery feasibility report was not available in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond the abstract-level findings.
Feasibility for physiological inputs beyond glucose remains unresolved; suitable signals and control mechanisms have not been established here.
The proposed human demonstrations still require application-specific choices of therapeutic endpoints, windows, allowable excursions, response times, duration and safe challenge protocols.

brief.title: Medicines that adjust their own effects
possible: People could take a medicine that senses changes in their body and adjusts its activity or release to keep its effect within a safe, effective range. For someone using insulin, blood sugar would guide that response from within the medicine itself, without an external controller.
why: Treatment could follow changing needs more closely, reducing the mismatch between too little medicine to help and too much to be safe. Building that response into the medicine could also reduce dependence on external sensors and control hardware.

sources.showed: A small human study found that software could adapt insulin delivery without users announcing meals. Participants spent more time with blood sugar in the target range, but the study had no comparison group.
sources.quote: A closed-loop algorithm that adjusts its own parameters and requires no meal announcement was feasible
sources.cited_for: The study supports the feasibility of adjusting treatment automatically in response to changing needs.
sources.not_established: The control came from external software, so it did not demonstrate a medicine regulating its own effects.

sources.showed: Brouillard reviewed animal studies of insulin that responds to blood sugar. Separate designs provided lasting control or protection against excessive insulin, alongside problems with delays, fading responses and unsafe release.
sources.quote: Their patch could maintain normoglycemia for ∼9 hours with no documented hypoglycemic events.
sources.cited_for: The commentary describes animal progress toward internally controlled insulin and obstacles to human use.
sources.not_established: The animal results do not establish sustained, safe control in humans.

shown: Zhang and colleagues reported normal blood sugar lasting about a week in minipigs given a responsive insulin complex. In separate work, Yang and colleagues reported protection against deliberately excessive insulin in animals using a patch. Brouillard's commentary describes these results.
Merck tested a responsive insulin molecule in humans, but it did not advance because of problems with its strength and how it behaved in the body.
missing: Human trials still need to demonstrate that internal sensing keeps a medicine's effect within a defined safe and effective range throughout treatment.
The response must remain fast and durable, avoid harmful release bursts, and account for drug that keeps acting after release slows.
Delivery materials must be safe for sustained use, and manufacturing must preserve reliable performance.

milestones.label: Two medicines control their effects using different body signals
milestones.explanation: Human studies would have to show two medicines sensing different body signals and internally keeping their effects within predefined ranges. This would establish breadth beyond blood sugar.

milestones.label: Internal control prevents excess while meeting rising needs
milestones.explanation: Safe challenge studies would have to show protection from excessive effects compared with a nonresponsive treatment, while preserving treatment as demand rises. This would distinguish feedback from simply giving less medicine.

milestones.label: Independent studies establish reliable control and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce control across people, batches and body conditions, defining delays, fading responses and delivery needs. This would establish when it works and when clinical help remains necessary.

uncertain: It remains unclear which body signals beyond blood sugar can reliably guide a medicine's response.
Each application needs its own target effect, acceptable range, response speed, treatment duration and safe challenge test.
Responsive materials may accumulate or cause harm during prolonged treatment.

page.title: Glucose-responsive insulin
page.definition: An insulin molecule or formulation senses glucose and adjusts its activity or release through chemical or physical mechanisms within the medicine. In people with diabetes, this response preserves glucose control while reducing hypoglycaemia, meaning abnormally low blood glucose, without an external dosing algorithm.

goal.need: In a survey published in 2024, approximately 20% of 2,074 US adults with type 1 diabetes reported a severe hypoglycaemic event during the preceding 12 months. Glucose-responsive insulin addresses the coupled requirements of sufficient insulin action and protection against excessive action. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings describe the surveyed sample rather than national prevalence.

figures.caption: Technology use and glycaemic control in the same survey
figures.note: HbA1c measures glycated haemoglobin and reflects average glucose exposure over approximately 2–3 months. Technology use and outcomes were self-reported.

statements.quote: JDRF has prioritized the development of a glucose-responsive insulin
statements.context: Its discovery-and-validation research call sought proof of concept in animal models of type 1 diabetes.

statements.quote: An injectable glucose sensitive insulin intended for once daily treatment.
statements.context: Description of project NN1644 in Annual Report 2024.

completion.title: FDA licenses a glucose-responsive insulin with a hypoglycaemia-risk-reduction claim.
completion.criterion: FDA approves a biologics licence for an insulin molecule or formulation meeting the definition above, with an authorised claim of reduced hypoglycaemia risk while preserving glycaemic control. The product and its manufacture must satisfy the applicable licensing requirements for safety, purity and potency. The claim applies to the population and treatment regimen evaluated in the approved application.
completion.set_by: FDA, biologics licensing under 21 CFR 601.2; hypoglycaemia-related claims are addressed in its May 2023 draft diabetes efficacy-endpoint guidance.
completion.threshold_quote: the manufactured product meets prescribed requirements of safety, purity, and potency
completion.basis: Licensure provides an external decision on the medicine and its manufacture. The hypoglycaemia claim addresses protection against excessive insulin action while retaining glucose control. FDA's published draft provides quantitative HbA1c conditions for interpreting that claim; those recommendations remain nonbinding and are not themselves an approval.

milestones.title: An insulin responds reversibly to glucose in laboratory tests.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate reversible glucose-dependent activity or release; JDRF gives no minimum switching ratio. Molecules: NNC2215 showed reversible switching and 3.2-fold higher receptor affinity at 20 versus 3 mmol/L glucose, measured in 3 independent experiments and published on 16 October 2024. Formulations: Zhang's complex showed pulsatile release during alternating exposure to 100 and 400 mg/dL glucose, with n=3 experiments, published on 6 December 2023.
milestones.set_by: Glucose-responsive-insulin proof-of-concept convention, explicitly stated in JDRF's 2014 research call and applied in the cited molecular and formulation studies.

milestones.title: A glucose-responsive insulin improves glycaemic control in an animal model of type 1 diabetes.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate improved glucose tolerance, reduced hypoglycaemia or another glycaemic improvement; JDRF specifies no minimum effect size. Molecules: NNC2215 reduced peak glucose during a glucose challenge to 18.3 versus 22.9 mmol/L with human insulin, with n=5 diabetic rats per group, published on 16 October 2024. Formulations: Zhang's complex produced approximately week-long glucose control in diabetic minipigs, with n=3 per group and a study-defined range of 50–200 mg/dL, published on 6 December 2023. These values are results, not milestone thresholds.
milestones.set_by: JDRF's 2014 animal proof-of-concept criteria and the comparative preclinical convention used in the cited studies.

milestones.title: A glucose-responsive insulin is administered to people in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: Reach first administration in an authorised human study assessing safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacological effects. Molecules: MK-2640 was studied in 36 healthy adults and a 16-person type 1 diabetes crossover study, published on 30 September 2018. Novo Nordisk listed its glucose-sensitive insulin programme as phase 1 completed in its second-quarter 2026 presentation; this company status report is not peer reviewed and supplies no sample size or efficacy result. No human dosing result was located for responsive delivery formulations.
milestones.set_by: FDA, the phase 1 definition in 21 CFR 312.21(a).
milestones.threshold_quote: initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans

milestones.title: A human study confirms a glucose-responsive insulin's prespecified response mechanism.
milestones.criterion: Meet a prespecified human proof-of-mechanism endpoint linking glucose concentration to the medicine's action or availability. Merck's MK-2640 protocol tested clearance at glucose clamps of 90 and 300 mg/dL. In 16 adults with type 1 diabetes, clearance decreased by a nonsignificant 6%; the glucose-infusion response changed, but the clearance endpoint was not met. Those clamp levels and that endpoint were specific to MK-2640. No successful prespecified mechanism endpoint was located for either implementation.
milestones.set_by: Clinical proof-of-mechanism convention, implemented in Merck's MK-2640 protocol NCT02269735; its clearance test was written for a soluble insulin molecule.
milestones.threshold_quote: by demonstrating a (glucose‐responsive) change in clearance between euglycemic and hyperglycemic conditions.

milestones.title: Controlled phase 2 studies establish a glucose-responsive insulin's efficacy and short-term risks.
milestones.criterion: Controlled studies in patients demonstrate preliminary efficacy for the intended indication and characterise common short-term adverse effects and risks. FDA's phase 2 definition sets no universal efficacy margin. For conventional insulin preparations, EMA recommends at least 4 weeks per preparation in crossover exploratory studies, with the 24-hour glucose profile as the preferred short-term endpoint. No qualifying result was located for either implementation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), and EMA, section 5.4.3 of its 2023 diabetes guideline. EMA's duration recommendation covers conventional insulin preparations; novel administration routes require separate scientific advice.
milestones.threshold_quote: The study duration should be at least 4 weeks with each insulin preparation for crossover designs

milestones.title: A glucose-responsive insulin reduces hypoglycaemia with an HbA1c difference of at most 0.1 percentage points.
milestones.criterion: Controlled confirmatory trials reduce severe hypoglycaemia requiring assistance, or an FDA-agreed composite of severe events and glucose below 54 mg/dL. The treatment-minus-comparator difference in HbA1c change has point estimate ≤0.1 percentage points and upper 95% confidence limit <0.3. FDA's draft generally recommends efficacy assessment after 6 months and durability assessment at 12 months; EMA requires at least 12-month efficacy and safety data for novel insulins. No qualifying result was located for either implementation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, section III.B of its May 2023 draft diabetes efficacy-endpoint guidance, which remains nonbinding; EMA, section 5.1 of its 2023 diabetes guideline, supplies the long-term evidence requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: the point estimate for the difference in change in A1C should be no greater than 0.1 percent.

not_found: Searches of FDA and EMA guidance and glucose-responsive-insulin research calls found no cross-drug completion standard for autonomous therapeutic-window control.
No FDA approval for a glucose-responsive insulin carrying a hypoglycaemia-risk-reduction claim was located.
The ClinicalTrials.gov record and API response for NCT06685185 could not be read in full, preventing verification of its participant count and detailed outcomes from that primary registry.
